A planning manager at a port logistics operator introduced a Claude workflow nine months ago for drafting vessel-scheduling change notifications to freight customers. The notifications require accurate berth times, vessel names, and cargo cut-off deadlines. Over nine months, errors in AI-drafted notifications have led to three missed cargo cut-offs by freight customers. Each missed cut-off resulted in a customer claim. Operations staff spend more time correcting Claude drafts than they would drafting manually.

What is the MOST appropriate course of action?

options.text: Provide additional training to the operations staff on how to verify berth times and vessel details before submitting Claude-drafted notifications to customers.
Switch to a more capable model tier to reduce the frequency of factual errors in scheduling details before continuing the workflow.

Sunset the workflow: the task requires precision in time-sensitive operational data that Claude cannot reliably provide without structured data integration, and the current manual-drafting approach has better outcomes.
Narrow the workflow scope to notifications with no cargo cut-off implications, retaining Claude only for notifications that carry no financial risk if incorrect.

explanation.correct: Three customer claims from missed cargo cut-offs in nine months — directly attributable to AI-drafted notifications — represents a pattern of serious customer harm from the workflow. The fact that staff now spend more time correcting drafts than drafting manually confirms that the workflow has negative net ROI. The root cause is structural: vessel-scheduling notifications require precise real-time operational data (berth times, cut-offs) that Claude cannot access without integration into the scheduling system. This is a task-fit problem, not a training or model problem.

distractors.A: Training staff to verify operational details adds verification overhead to a workflow that already costs more in correction time than manual drafting. More training does not resolve the root cause: Claude does not have access to the real-time scheduling data required for accurate notifications.
distractors.B: A more capable model tier will not reduce factual errors caused by missing structured data inputs. Claude cannot know the correct berth time if that information is not in the prompt. Model tier is not the variable causing the errors.
distractors.D: Narrowing scope to 'no cut-off implications' may reduce harm but defines the remaining use cases so narrowly that the workflow delivers negligible value. And the port's operation means most scheduling changes have some downstream time dependency.

explanation.concept:
**Task-fit sunsetting criterion**: certain tasks are structurally unsuited to AI assistance in the current form because they require precise, real-time operational data that must be injected from a system of record — not recalled from training or inferred from context. Vessel scheduling is an example: the correct berth time is in the port management system, not in Claude's context, unless it is explicitly provided.

The appropriate long-term solution may be a properly integrated workflow where scheduling data is piped into the prompt. Until that integration exists, the correct decision is to stop the workflow causing customer harm.
explanation.examTip: When a workflow is causing **repeated, measurable customer harm** and the root cause is structural (missing data the model cannot access), the correct decision is **sunset** — not training, model upgrade, or scope narrowing. Scope narrowing delays a decision the harm evidence demands. The correct long-term approach (data integration) is a different project, not a reason to continue the harmful workflow.

topic: Scaling a content workflow from team to organisation
stem:
A content strategy VP at a streaming media company is scaling a Claude-assisted content-briefing workflow from her five-person editorial team to all 40 content managers across three regional offices. The editorial team's workflow has been highly effective for six months and uses a refined prompt template and a shared Project with content standards.

Which TWO scaling elements are MOST critical to get right before the forty-person rollout begins? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Translate the editorial team's refined prompt template and Project instructions into written documentation that explains not just what the template says but why each element was designed that way, so regional managers can adapt it intelligently.
Appoint one champion in each regional office who has already reviewed the editorial team's workflow, received live coaching from a member of the editorial team, and can answer questions locally.
Conduct a satisfaction survey of the editorial team to collect a Net Promoter Score for the workflow before rolling it out, to use as baseline evidence of team endorsement.
Replace the Project custom instructions with a more detailed version that covers every possible content briefing scenario the regional offices might encounter.
Require the 40 content managers to complete a two-week prompt-engineering certification before accessing the shared Project.

explanation.correct: **A (documented template rationale)** enables intelligent adaptation: regional offices operate in different markets with different content conventions. A template explanation that covers the reasoning behind each design choice allows managers to adapt the template to their context without inadvertently removing the elements that make it effective. **B (per-office champions with live coaching)** provides the sustained local support structure that a forty-person multi-office rollout requires. Champions who have received live editorial-team coaching can answer regional questions with accurate context.

distractors.C: An NPS survey of the five-person editorial team generates a data point that is neither statistically meaningful at five respondents nor relevant to the forty-person rollout design. It is an administrative step that does not improve rollout quality.
distractors.D: Expanding the Project instructions to cover every possible scenario creates a bloated instruction set that may conflict with itself and makes the Project harder to maintain. The editorial team's refined instructions work precisely because they focus on the most important guidance, not every edge case.
distractors.E: A two-week certification before access delays the rollout by at least two weeks and is disproportionate to the skill required to use a well-designed prompt template. The editorial team's success was built on a good template, not on advanced prompt-engineering certification.

explanation.concept:
**Scaling a proven workflow to a larger, distributed population** requires:
1. **Rationale documentation** so recipients can adapt intelligently rather than follow blindly
2. **Distributed support structure** so questions get answered in context without requiring all support to flow through the originating team
3. **Proportionate enablement** — sophisticated enough to produce competency, not so heavy that it delays rollout

The editorial team's six months of refinement is the asset being scaled. The goal is to transfer both the artefact (template) and the knowledge behind it (rationale) efficiently.
explanation.examTip: When scaling a proven workflow to a larger distributed population, the two critical elements are **rationale documentation** (so recipients can adapt without breaking the design) and **local champions** (so support scales with the user population). NPS surveys (C), over-specified instructions (D), and heavy certification requirements (E) are all distractor patterns that add administrative overhead without improving the rollout's probability of success.

topic: Measuring AI programme impact on operational decisions
stem:
An asset management head at a transmission system operator has run a Claude programme for twelve months, using the tool to synthesise asset condition reports and maintenance prioritisation recommendations for 200 transmission assets. He presents the programme's metrics to the executive leadership team: Claude sessions run per month, analyst satisfaction scores, and reduction in synthesis time per asset. The operations director asks: 'Has any of this changed how we make maintenance decisions or reduced our unplanned outages?'

What does this question reveal about the programme's value evidence?

options.text: The operations director is applying an unreasonably short timeframe — twelve months is insufficient to observe statistically meaningful changes in unplanned outage rates for transmission infrastructure.
The operations director should be directed to the analyst satisfaction scores, which provide indirect evidence of improved decision-making quality through the analysts who make maintenance decisions.
The operations director is conflating operational reliability with AI programme contribution; unplanned outage rates depend on many variables beyond the quality of maintenance prioritisation.

The programme tracked tool adoption and efficiency gains but collected no evidence of whether synthesised recommendations were acted on, whether maintenance decision quality improved, or whether asset reliability outcomes changed — leaving the core operational value question unanswered.

explanation.correct: The operations director's question exposes a measurement gap: all three of the programme's metrics (session counts, satisfaction, synthesis time) measure the tool's use and its efficiency at the synthesis task, but none connect to the purpose for which the synthesis was done — better maintenance decisions and, ultimately, reduced unplanned outages. The programme can demonstrate that analysts used Claude, liked it, and synthesised faster, but cannot answer whether any of that synthesis influenced an actual maintenance decision or improved an asset reliability outcome. This is the activity-to-impact measurement gap.

distractors.A: Twelve months is a reasonable window to observe changes in maintenance decisions and to begin tracking whether synthesised recommendations were acted on. It is admittedly short for statistical significance in outage rates, but the operations director's question includes maintenance decision quality, which is observable within twelve months. The timeframe criticism is partially valid but deflects from the measurement gap.
distractors.B: Analyst satisfaction scores measure how analysts feel about the tool — they do not indicate that decisions improved or that synthesised recommendations were used to change maintenance priorities. Satisfaction is a leading indicator of adoption, not evidence of decision quality.
distractors.C: The operations director is not conflating reliability with AI contribution — she is correctly asking whether the AI contribution had any observable effect. Acknowledging that multiple variables affect reliability is accurate, but it is also the standard deflection for avoiding a direct measurement commitment. The correct response to 'did this change our decisions?' is to measure decisions, not to note that outage rates have multiple causes.

explanation.concept:
**Activity-to-impact measurement chain** for decision-support AI programmes:
1. **Activity layer**: sessions run, time per synthesis (collected)
2. **Behaviour layer**: were synthesised recommendations reviewed by decision-makers? (not collected)
3. **Decision layer**: did maintenance priorities change based on synthesised output? (not collected)
4. **Outcome layer**: did asset reliability or unplanned outage rates change? (not collected)

The programme measured only layer 1. The operations director is asking for layers 3 and 4. Layers 2 and 3 are the missing evidence that would connect the programme's activity to the business outcome.
explanation.examTip: This **hard item** tests whether you identify the **activity-to-impact gap** rather than deflecting with timeframe (A), conflation (C), or indirect evidence (B). When a decision-support AI programme can show adoption and efficiency but cannot answer 'did this change decisions?', the measurement design stopped at the activity layer. The correct diagnosis names that gap — session counts and satisfaction scores do not answer whether the synthesised output was used to make better maintenance calls.

stem:
A change programme lead at a semiconductor manufacturer has just completed a successful two-month pilot of a Claude-assisted specification documentation workflow with eight process engineers. The pilot demonstrated strong quality and a 35% time reduction. She has approval to roll out to the full 60-person engineering team and has drafted a change management plan. Before launching, she realises her plan assumes all 60 engineers have the same level of AI familiarity as the eight pilot engineers — who self-selected because they were already interested in AI tools.

What should the change programme lead do NEXT?

options.text: Proceed with the rollout as planned; the 35% time reduction data will be compelling enough to overcome any familiarity gap during deployment.
Survey the 52 non-pilot engineers to assess their current AI familiarity level, prior tool experience, and specific concerns before finalising the change management and enablement plan.
Restrict the rollout to engineers who volunteer first, replicating the self-selection dynamic of the pilot until the majority choose to participate organically.

Revise the change management plan to include a tiered enablement track: a lighter track for engineers with prior AI tool experience and a more supported track for those without, then proceed with rollout.

explanation.correct: The lead has identified a specific plan flaw: the enablement assumptions do not match the population being served. The correct next step is to fix the flaw before launching — by revising the plan to include a tiered enablement approach that serves both experienced and inexperienced engineers appropriately. This is both a diagnostic insight and a plan fix in one step, which is more efficient than surveying first (B) and then revising.

distractors.A: Proceeding with a known planning flaw because the ROI data is strong is a risk management error. Strong pilot results do not neutralise an enablement mismatch. Unexperienced engineers who struggle without the right support level will experience frustration that ROI data does not prevent.
distractors.B: Surveying the 52 engineers first is a valid diagnostic step, but the lead already has enough information to diagnose the flaw (the pilot used self-selected AI-interested engineers) without needing to survey. A survey adds two to three weeks before any revision can begin. Proceeding directly to a tiered plan revision is more efficient.
distractors.C: Restricting to volunteers replicates the pilot dynamic indefinitely and never achieves the full 60-person rollout approval she was given. Self-selection excludes the engineers who most need the supported track and creates an unequal adoption pattern.

explanation.concept:
**Self-selection bias in pilot populations** is one of the most common scaling errors. Pilot participants who volunteer are typically the most motivated, most technically comfortable, and least likely to struggle. Their results cannot be directly extrapolated to the full population, which includes engineers who did not volunteer and may have lower familiarity, more scepticism, or more complex concerns.

A tiered enablement approach — lighter support for the experienced, more support for the inexperienced — is the standard design response when the deployment population is heterogeneous in AI familiarity.
explanation.examTip: When the stem reveals that a **pilot used self-selected enthusiasts** and the full deployment population is more diverse in familiarity or motivation, the correct next step is to **adjust the change management or enablement plan before launching** — not proceed hoping the ROI data compensates (A), not survey first when the diagnosis is already clear (B), not restrict to volunteers indefinitely (C). Fix the identified flaw, then proceed.

topic: ROI measurement for research grant programmes
stem:
A grants manager at a cancer research hospital has used Claude for ten months to help draft grant applications. Over that period, the hospital submitted 18% more grant applications than the prior year and its success rate held steady at 32%. She is preparing a presentation to the hospital's development committee on the ROI of her AI programme.

How should she frame the ten-month results to make the strongest credible ROI case?

options.text: Focus on the 18% application volume increase alone, since the development committee primarily cares about output volume.
Present the success rate as the primary ROI metric because a stable 32% rate demonstrates that quality was not sacrificed for volume.

Calculate the financial value of the additional applications submitted at the historical success rate, and connect it to the programme's cost, to show expected grant revenue generated per dollar invested.
Avoid presenting any financial figures because grant award amounts vary widely and attributing specific revenue to Claude would overstate the programme's contribution.

explanation.correct: The strongest ROI case connects the operational metric (18% more applications) to financial value using the known success rate (32%) as a converter. Expected additional revenue = additional applications × success rate × average grant value. This gives the development committee a dollar figure they can compare to the programme's cost, producing a genuine ROI ratio rather than an operational metric without a value anchor. Stable quality (32% success rate) is the quality-preservation evidence that makes the volume claim credible.

distractors.A: Volume alone is an activity metric — it tells the committee output went up but not what that output is worth. A development committee allocating budget needs a value measure, not a volume measure, to make a funding decision.
distractors.B: Success rate alone is a quality metric — it tells the committee quality held, but not what additional applications are worth or whether the programme paid for itself. Quality preservation is a necessary component of the ROI case, not the primary ROI metric.
distractors.D: Avoiding financial figures because individual grant amounts vary is an unnecessary conservatism. Average grant values are knowable and appropriate for an expected-value calculation. Withholding a reasonable financial projection because it involves an average leaves the committee without the most useful information.

explanation.concept:
**Connecting operational metrics to financial value** is the final step in a complete ROI case:
1. **Operational metric**: 18% more applications
2. **Quality preservation metric**: 32% success rate held steady
3. **Financial value calculation**: additional apps × 32% × average grant value = expected additional revenue
4. **ROI ratio**: expected additional revenue ÷ programme cost

The success rate is the quality-preservation evidence that makes the volume claim defensible. Without it, the committee might assume the additional applications were lower quality. With it, the full value chain is complete.
explanation.examTip: A complete ROI case for an AI programme always requires both a **value metric** and a **quality-preservation metric**. Volume alone (A) and quality alone (B) are each incomplete. The correct approach uses the quality metric to validate the volume claim and then converts the volume metric to financial value. The three-step chain is: volume × quality rate × value per unit = total value.

topic: Prompt library governance at enterprise scale
stem:
A knowledge management VP at a global management consulting firm is designing a firm-wide prompt library for 2,000 consultants across 15 practice areas. The library must be high-quality, kept current as client industry standards evolve, and used consistently rather than ignored. The VP has a programme management team of three people.

Which TWO governance mechanisms are MOST essential to sustaining the library's quality and adoption over a twelve-month horizon? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Assign a named prompt steward in each of the 15 practice areas who owns the quality and currency of that practice's templates, with a quarterly review cycle and a mechanism to propose updates.
Require all 2,000 consultants to submit every client deliverable prompt to the programme team for review before use, to maintain quality control.
Run a bi-annual firm-wide survey asking consultants how satisfied they are with the library to track engagement.

Embed the prompt library into the firm's existing knowledge management platform so consultants encounter it as part of their natural workflow rather than as a separate tool they must remember to visit.

Publish monthly usage analytics to practice area leads showing which templates are being used, which are being skipped, and which templates prompted the most subsequent editing — providing a usage signal for quality issues.

explanation.correct: **A (practice-area stewards with quarterly review)** is the only governance mechanism that scales quality maintenance to 15 practice areas without requiring the three-person programme team to own all content. Stewards have the domain knowledge to evaluate whether templates reflect current industry standards, and a quarterly review cycle creates a regular update cadence. **D (embedding in existing workflow)** addresses the adoption risk: a library that consultants must visit separately will not be used consistently. Integration into the firm's existing knowledge management platform makes the library a default resource rather than an optional one.

distractors.B: Requiring 2,000 consultants to submit every prompt for review before use is operationally impossible for a three-person team. At any reasonable volume, this creates a bottleneck that would make the library unusable and guarantee non-adoption.
distractors.C: A bi-annual satisfaction survey provides feedback twice per year with a significant lag. It does not provide the quality signals or the usage signals needed to maintain a library that consultants are using daily for client work.
distractors.E: Monthly usage analytics is a useful signal but is a monitoring tool, not a maintenance mechanism. Analytics can indicate which templates have problems; they do not fix those problems. Without stewards accountable for acting on the signals, analytics generate awareness without resolution.

explanation.concept:
**Enterprise-scale prompt library governance** requires two distinct systems:
1. **Quality maintenance system** — who is responsible for keeping content current, on what cycle, and with what update authority (stewards with domain expertise)
2. **Adoption system** — how the library reaches consultants in their natural workflow rather than requiring deliberate navigation to a separate resource

A high-quality library that requires a separate login and a deliberate navigation decision will underperform a lower-quality library embedded in the workflow consultants already use. Adoption is as critical as quality maintenance.
explanation.examTip: This **hard item** tests whether you can identify the two distinct failure modes of a large prompt library: **quality decay** (solved by stewards) and **adoption failure** (solved by workflow integration). Options B, C, and E each address a related but different problem — B is a quality gate (too expensive), C is feedback (too slow), E is monitoring (no maintenance). The correct pair addresses both primary failure modes directly.

topic: Pilot design for a public agency
stem:
An information management lead at a state environmental agency wants to run a first Claude pilot for her team of ten environmental permit analysts. The analysts review and respond to permit applications from industrial facilities. She has two candidate use cases: drafting acknowledgement letters to permit applicants, and drafting technical deficiency notices identifying missing information in incomplete applications.

Which is the BETTER first pilot use case for a public agency with no prior AI experience?

options.text: Acknowledgement letters, because they are low-stakes, formulaic in structure, and errors can be corrected before causing regulatory or stakeholder harm — giving the team a safe learning environment.
Technical deficiency notices, because the high complexity of the task will force analysts to engage deeply with the tool and develop stronger prompting skills more quickly.
Technical deficiency notices, because demonstrating Claude's capability on a complex regulatory task will make a stronger ROI case to the agency director.
Both simultaneously, because a public agency has an obligation to evaluate AI tools comprehensively before committing to any single use case.

explanation.correct: Acknowledgement letters are the correct first pilot for a team with no prior AI experience because they are low-stakes and highly reviewable — any error is caught before the letter leaves the agency, and an incorrect acknowledgement letter causes no regulatory harm. The team can focus on learning the tool, developing effective prompts, and building confidence before tackling the more consequential and variable technical deficiency notices.

distractors.B: A challenging first use case does not accelerate skill development — it accelerates frustration and early abandonment. Analysts who struggle with complex outputs in their first AI experience associate the tool with difficulty rather than with productivity. Start simple; build to complex.
distractors.C: A strong ROI case for the agency director is a business-development argument, not a pilot-design criterion. Pilots exist to generate learning safely. Choosing a complex high-stakes use case to impress leadership before the team is ready is a common first-pilot failure mode.
distractors.D: A public-agency obligation to comprehensive evaluation does not require simultaneous parallel pilots. Comprehensive evaluation can be sequential. Parallel pilots split the team's learning focus and the manager's optimisation attention.

explanation.concept:
**First-pilot design for teams with no prior AI experience** requires additional conservatism:
- The first use case should be forgiving of errors (low stakes, high reviewability)
- Success on the first use case builds the confidence and appetite for more complex use cases
- Failure or frustration on the first use case creates lasting negative associations that are harder to reverse than slow adoption

The acknowledgement-letter-to-deficiency-notice progression is a classic low-to-high complexity ramp that is appropriate for any team new to AI-assisted work.
explanation.examTip: Easy pilot items test whether you select the use case that **protects the team's first experience** over the use case that **maximises the impressive result**. For a team with no prior AI experience, start with the simplest, lowest-stakes task type. The first experience shapes adoption attitudes more than any subsequent communication or mandate.

topic: Enablement programme design for technical trainers
stem:
An L&D director at a telecom equipment vendor is designing Claude enablement for 30 technical trainers who deliver product training to enterprise customers. Trainers are expert communicators with deep product knowledge but varying comfort with AI. The L&D director's goal: every trainer can independently use Claude to customise standard training decks for specific customer contexts within two weeks of programme launch.

Which enablement design would MOST reliably achieve this specific goal?

options.text: Assign all 30 trainers a self-paced e-learning course covering Claude prompting theory and have them demonstrate completion before accessing any shared templates.

Provide each trainer with a ready-to-use prompt template for training deck customisation, run a ninety-minute hands-on session where each trainer customises one real deck for an upcoming customer, and designate two AI-confident trainers as on-call peers for the first two weeks.
Deploy a locked Claude interface pre-loaded with a customisation workflow, so trainers simply enter customer details and receive a customised deck without needing to learn prompting skills.
Require all 30 trainers to complete a four-hour live workshop covering Claude architecture, prompting best practices, and common failure modes before using the tool on any real content.

explanation.correct: Option B is the only design that achieves the specific stated goal — independent customisation of real training decks within two weeks — at the right effort level. The template removes the prompt-design burden; the ninety-minute session with a real upcoming customer produces immediate, task-specific skill; and the on-call peer support ensures questions during the first two weeks of independent use are answered without waiting for a scheduled session. This is the minimum sufficient enablement for the stated goal.

distractors.A: E-learning completion as a prerequisite before template access delays the goal by however long the course takes and withholds the most useful learning resource (the template and real practice) until after the theoretical foundation is built. For expert communicators, the template-first approach is more efficient.
distractors.C: A locked interface solves the immediate customisation problem but builds no independent prompting capability. When trainers encounter a customisation need outside the locked interface's scope — a different deck format, an unusual customer context — they have no recourse. Locked interfaces serve consistency goals, not capability goals.
distractors.D: A four-hour architecture and best-practices workshop is disproportionate to the stated goal of customising training decks. Expert communicators with deep product knowledge need task-specific practice, not four hours of theoretical grounding before touching real content.

explanation.concept:
**Goal-matched enablement design** starts from the specific goal and works backward to the minimum sufficient enablement:
- Goal: independently customise training decks within two weeks
- Required skills: follow a prompt template; adapt it for customer context; evaluate output quality
- Minimum enablement: template + one real-task practice session + just-in-time support for the first two weeks

Over-investing in conceptual grounding (A, D) or eliminating skill development entirely (C) both fail to achieve the stated goal. B achieves it with the least overhead.
explanation.examTip: This **hard item** tests goal-matched enablement design. All four options are plausible enablement approaches in general. The discriminator is the specific stated goal — 'independent use within two weeks.' A (e-learning prerequisite), C (locked interface), and D (long theory workshop) each fail the goal on a different dimension. B is the only option that achieves the goal at the right timing and capability level simultaneously.

stem:
A store operations VP at an independent grocery chain is rolling out a Claude workflow for drafting weekly store communication briefings to 35 store managers. After six weeks, 12 managers are active users and 23 have tried it once but reverted to drafting manually. Exit interviews reveal that the 23 managers felt the drafts were 'too generic' and 'didn't sound like they came from someone who knows our stores.'

What is the MOST direct cause of this reversion and how should the VP address it?

options.text: The 23 managers lack sufficient literacy to prompt Claude effectively, and a mandatory training programme should be run before the rollout continues.

The shared prompt template does not include fields for store-specific context — local events, team names, seasonal factors — so managers receive generic drafts that feel impersonal, and the template should be redesigned with required context fields.
Claude is fundamentally unsuited to drafting communication that requires store-level context, and the workflow should be narrowed to communications with no local customisation.
The managers' preference for manual drafting is driven by habit rather than quality, and more usage over time will naturally produce personalisation as they develop their own prompting habits.

explanation.correct: The managers' complaint — 'too generic, doesn't know our stores' — is the direct feedback that the template is not prompting them to inject store-specific context. The template is likely a generic 'draft a briefing' prompt without required fields for local events, team names, seasonal factors, or store-specific issues. Redesigning the template to include explicit context fields converts it from a generic prompt into a scaffold that produces personalised output when managers fill in their store's details.

distractors.A: The managers are experienced communicators who successfully draft briefings manually. The skill gap is not communication ability but knowing that they need to inject store-specific context into the Claude prompt. This is a template design problem, not a training problem.
distractors.C: Claude can absolutely incorporate store-specific context — if that context is in the prompt. The issue is not model suitability; it is a template design that does not require managers to provide local context. Generic prompt = generic output; context-rich prompt = context-rich output.
distractors.D: If managers reverted after one session and specifically cited generic output as the reason, assuming habit will resolve the problem over time misattributes a design gap to a behavioural one. Managers will not naturally develop personalisation habits around a template that does not ask them for personalising information.

explanation.concept:
**Reversion from AI workflows** after a single use almost always traces to a quality gap on the first attempt. When the stated reason is 'too generic,' the template design is the root cause: required-fill fields for local or context-specific information are missing.

The fix: redesign the template with mandatory context fields that the user must complete before Claude can produce a personalised output. Required fields prevent the 'submit the template as-is' behaviour that produces generic output.
explanation.examTip: The phrase 'too generic, didn't sound like it came from someone who knows our stores' is the specific diagnostic signal of a **template missing required-fill context fields**. This is a template redesign problem, not a training problem, a model problem, or a habit problem. When managers revert after one use citing generic output, check the template for missing context fields before assuming any other cause.

stem:
An actuarial operations head at a life insurer has run a Claude-assisted workflow for drafting actuarial assumption documentation for eighteen months. The workflow saves time on initial drafts but auditors have noted that assumption justifications frequently require significant rework during the annual reserve review — more so than before Claude was adopted. The chief actuary and head of internal audit are both expressing concern.

Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate given this evidence? (Choose TWO)

options.text: Continue the workflow but add a senior actuary review step before any assumption documentation enters the audit process, accepting the rework cost as a quality control measure.
Expand the workflow to cover more actuarial documentation types so that the time savings across a larger scope justify the rework cost in assumption justifications.
Suspend the workflow for assumption justification documentation pending a root-cause review that includes the auditors and senior actuaries whose concerns are on record.

Conduct a structured post-mortem examining whether the observed rework increase is attributable to the AI workflow or to other factors (reviewer changes, assumption complexity increases, updated audit standards) that coincided with deployment.
Present the time savings data to the chief actuary as evidence that the programme is net positive despite the rework increase, and request more time before any structural decision.

explanation.correct: **C (suspend assumption justification documentation)** removes the active source of the concern while the investigation proceeds. With both the chief actuary and head of internal audit expressing concern, continuing to generate documentation that requires significant rework during the reserve review creates ongoing regulatory and audit risk. **D (structured post-mortem with causality analysis)** is the correct investigation because the rework increase might be attributable to the workflow, to changed audit standards, or to increased assumption complexity — and the correct response depends entirely on which cause is responsible.

distractors.A: Adding a senior actuary review step accepts the rework cost as permanent and does not address whether the workflow is the cause. If the workflow is producing structurally inadequate assumption justifications, a review step catches them but does not fix the root cause.
distractors.B: Expanding scope of a workflow that is generating audit concerns about documentation quality would amplify the problem across more documentation types. Expanding before understanding the root cause is the opposite of appropriate risk management.
distractors.E: Presenting time savings to the chief actuary when both she and the head of internal audit have expressed documented quality concerns is a change-management error. The concerns are on record; presenting efficiency data as a counterargument without addressing the quality concern will damage trust and credibility.

explanation.concept:
**Suspension-and-investigation** is the appropriate response when:
- An AI workflow is implicated in a quality problem in a regulated, audit-sensitive context
- Two senior stakeholders with relevant oversight authority have expressed documented concerns
- The causal relationship between the workflow and the quality problem has not been established

Suspension protects the organisation while the cause is investigated. The investigation must include both the workflow's potential contribution and alternative explanations — confirming or ruling out causality before the appropriate fix can be selected.
explanation.examTip: This **hard item** requires combining two actions from five options. The key discrimination: E (present efficiency data to the chief actuary) is clearly wrong when she is one of the concerned parties. B (expand scope) amplifies risk. A (add review step) accepts the problem without fixing it. The correct pair is the only one that both **stops the risk** (C) and **investigates the cause** (D) — which are the two necessary conditions for a defensible response in a regulated audit context.

topic: Prompt templates for field staff communications
stem:
An executive director at a youth development NGO wants her three programme officers to use Claude consistently for drafting volunteer appreciation notes, programme update newsletters, and partnership renewal letters. Each officer currently drafts these differently, and the ED spends time editing them to align voice and structure before distribution.

What is the MOST efficient way to reduce the ED's editing burden while preserving each officer's ability to personalise the content?

options.text: Build a separate prompt template for each of the three document types, each specifying the required structure, voice, and key message elements, and share them with all three programme officers as the starting point for each draft.
Ask the programme officers to route all drafts through the ED for approval before distribution, ensuring quality control remains centralised.
Train the three programme officers on advanced prompting techniques over a two-day workshop so they can independently develop their own consistent prompt approaches.
Create a single universal Claude prompt covering all three document types and ask officers to specify which document they need at the start of each session.

explanation.correct: Three separate templates — one per document type — encode the required structure, voice, and key message elements for each distinct communication. Officers start from a consistent scaffold and fill in the personalising content for their specific programme, volunteer, or partner. The ED's editing burden drops because structural and tonal variation is eliminated at the source. Officers retain the ability to personalise the specific content within the consistent framework.

distractors.B: Centralising all approvals through the ED maintains quality control but does not reduce her workload — it formulates it as a permanent review role rather than an editing role. The workload cause (structural and tonal variation) is unchanged.
distractors.C: A two-day prompting workshop develops general skill but does not produce a shared quality standard. Officers who each develop their 'own consistent approach' may still diverge from each other. The ED needs a shared standard across the three officers, not three individually consistent approaches.
distractors.D: A single universal prompt for all three document types produces an over-broad instruction set that either under-specifies each document type (producing generic output) or becomes too complex to interpret consistently. Three distinct document types with distinct audiences and purposes warrant three distinct templates.

explanation.concept:
**Template architecture for multiple document types** follows a one-template-per-document-type structure when the documents have distinct audiences, purposes, and structural requirements (as volunteer appreciation notes, newsletters, and partnership letters do).

A shared template library for a small team delivers:
- Consistent structure across all staff for each document type
- Consistent voice that reduces ED editing
- Officer ability to personalise specific content within the scaffold
- Zero platform infrastructure required — just shared documents

This is the prompt-layer equivalent of a communications style guide.
explanation.examTip: Easy items on template architecture often include a single-universal-template option (D) that seems efficient. Resist it when the document types have different audiences and purposes. The correct architecture is **one template per distinct document type**. A universal template that tries to serve all document types produces templates that serve none of them well.
